s: SELECT * returns 61 columns; Power Query keeps 9. Select only those: less I/O, less network, and the query can be covered by an index.

CONVERT(varchar, o.OrderID) = l.OrderID: mismatched join types force a conversion on every row and prevent seeks. Make both sides the same type (ask Kenji to fix the column), or convert the smaller side once.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) = 2026 isn't sargable: use OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2027-01-01' so the OrderDate index can seek.
UPPER(o.Status) = 'COMPLETED': the column is already upper case in the data; compare directly (or fix collation) so it can be part of an index.
The correlated COUNT(*) on Returns runs 41 million times: replace with NOT EXISTS, which the optimiser runs as one anti-join and can stop at the first match.
ORDER BY is pointless for Power BI (it doesn't preserve order) and adds a sort over millions of rows: remove it.
Indexes to request: nonclustered on Orders(Status, OrderDate) INCLUDE (CustomerID, Channel, SalesRegionKey, Currency); and on Returns(OrderID, LineNo). Then check the plan again.
Downstream: refresh drops from ~22 minutes to minutes; with a foldable date range, incremental refresh can push RangeStart/RangeEnd filters to the source and refresh only recent partitions.

code.title: Original logic vs rewrite: same rows (portable version run in CI)
src: JOIN orders AS o ON o.OrderID = l.OrderID
WHERE SUBSTRING(CAST(o.OrderDate AS VARCHAR(10)), 1, 4) = '2026'        -- stands in for YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026
AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM returns AS r WHERE r.OrderID = l.OrderID AND r."LineNo" = l."LineNo") = 0
JOIN orders AS o ON o.OrderID = l.OrderID
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND o.OrderDate < '2027-01-01'      -- sargable range
AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM returns AS r WHERE r.OrderID = l.OrderID AND r."LineNo" = l."LineNo")
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM original) AS OriginalRows,

code.title: The rewrite for SQL Server
src: SELECT l.OrderID, l.[LineNo], o.OrderDate, o.PostingDate, o.CustomerID, o.Channel,
o.SalesRegionKey, l.ProductKey, l.Qty, l.UnitPrice, l.DiscountPct, o.Currency
ON o.OrderID = l.OrderID                -- after fixing OrderLines.OrderID to int
AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Returns AS r WHERE r.OrderID = l.OrderID AND r.[LineNo] = l.[LineNo]);
ON dbo.Orders (Status, OrderDate) INCLUDE (PostingDate, CustomerID, Channel, SalesRegionKey, Currency);
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Returns_OrderLine ON dbo.Returns (OrderID, [LineNo]);

sql-tune-0.check: Both return {{sql_slow_rows|int}} rows on the company pack. On SQL Server, expect seeks instead of scans and no per-row Returns scan.
sql-tune-0.note: The original query also didn't exclude duplicates or the test customer. A faster query that returns wrong rows is still wrong: use vw_FactSales from the previous topic as the base.
sql-tune-0.verify: Row equivalence executed in CI against SQLite; the T-SQL block and index advice are not executed.

s: Seek: the explicit date range; LIKE 'ava.%' (prefix).
CONVERT(date, datetime2col) = constant: SQL Server treats this as a sargable range internally, a documented exception, but don't rely on it for other functions.

No seek: YEAR(OrderDate) → rewrite as a range; LOWER(Email) → use a case-insensitive collation (default) and compare directly, or a persisted computed column with an index; LIKE '%@example.com' → can't seek; store the domain in its own column if it's queried often.
sql-tune-1.check: Seekable: range, prefix LIKE, CONVERT(date) on datetime2. Not: YEAR(), LOWER(), leading wildcard.

s: Shared business rules go as far upstream as possible: deduplication, currency conversion and test-customer exclusion in the warehouse view (folds, reused by every model, one fix).
Shape-only changes that the source can't do: Power Query, as long as folding is preserved or the table is small.
Anything that depends on filter context is a measure: days since last order changes with the date filter.
Display formatting belongs in the model (format strings), not in data.
Rule: transform as far upstream as possible, as far downstream as necessary.
tbl: Shared rule; everyone gets the same rows
Data quality rule for every consumer
